title: CompTIA Security+
tagline: Security+ SY0-701 prep across all five exam domains: security concepts, threats and mitigations, security architecture, security operations, and governance/risk/compliance — learned through scored practice scenarios.
disclaimer: Independent training material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by CompTIA. Confers no certification. All scenarios are original practice content; no CompTIA exam content is reproduced.

domains.name: General Security Concepts
domains.summary: The CIA triad, security control types, threat actors, attack vectors, and social engineering — the vocabulary every Security+ objective builds on.

scenarios.title: The Triad at the Bedside
scenarios.situation: You are the junior analyst on call for a regional hospital's security team. The electronic health record (EHR) system holds medication administration records — the data nurses rely on to dose patients. Last quarter the hospital suffered two incidents: a ransomware outage that took the EHR offline for 6 hours in the ER, and a breach in which an attacker exported 40,000 patient records. Leadership now asks which leg of the CIA triad should drive the top-funded control for the medication dosing data itself.
scenarios.prompt: Which principle of the CIA triad should take priority for protecting the medication dosing records, and why?
evidence: dosing data
Nurses dose insulin and anticoagulants directly from these records. A single altered value can cause a fatal overdose — there is no second human check.
outage impact
During the 6-hour EHR outage, the ER diverted ambulances and delayed care, but no patient received the wrong medication.
breach impact
The exported records triggered breach-notification costs and reputational damage, but no patient's treatment was altered.
choices: Confidentiality — encrypt the records and audit every access, because the breach affected 40,000 patients
Integrity — protect the accuracy and trustworthiness of dosing values with checksums, input validation, and strict change controls
Availability — maximize EHR uptime with clustering and failover, because the outage diverted ambulances
Non-repudiation — log every clinician action so no one can deny changing a dose
scenarios.why: All three legs matter, but the question asks about the dosing data itself. Altered medication data kills patients even when the system is up and the data is private — integrity is the patient-safety-critical property. Checksums, digital signatures, role-based change controls, and validation rules directly protect data accuracy. Confidentiality addresses the breach, availability addresses the outage, and non-repudiation supports accountability, but none of them stops a wrong dose.
scenarios.hint: Ask what happens if each property fails for the dosing values specifically: leaked (bad), unavailable (bad), wrong (fatal).
objectives: Apply the CIA triad to a real system
Prioritize controls by impact on the asset

scenarios.title: Name the Actor
scenarios.situation: A mid-size manufacturer of industrial sensors reports a breach. The timeline: spear-phishing emails tailored to two R&D engineers, a custom backdoor never seen in public malware feeds, 14 months of quiet dwell time, and slow exfiltration of CAD designs to infrastructure that rotates across bulletproof hosting providers. No ransom demand, no data leak site, no financial fraud. The board asks whether this looks like ransomware affiliates or something else.
scenarios.prompt: Which threat actor profile best fits this campaign?
evidence: tooling
The backdoor is custom-built, signed with a stolen code-signing certificate, and has no overlap with commodity crimeware kits.
objective
Only R&D design files were taken — finance, HR, and customer payment systems were untouched.
tempo
The intruders moved slowly, used living-off-the-land binaries, and maintained access for over a year without monetizing it.
choices: Organized crime — the stolen certificate and long dwell time are typical of ransomware affiliates
Hacktivists — the slow exfiltration suggests an ideological motive against the manufacturer
Nation-state / advanced persistent threat (APT) — custom tooling, espionage objective, and patience point to state-sponsored IP theft
Malicious insider — only someone inside could have known which engineers held the CAD files
scenarios.why: Custom malware, a stolen code-signing certificate, 14 months of dwell, living-off-the-land tradecraft, and theft of intellectual property with no monetization are the classic nation-state espionage pattern. Organized crime monetizes quickly (ransomware, fraud); hacktivists deface or leak for publicity; and while an insider could provide targeting, the external infrastructure and custom tooling point to an external APT.
scenarios.hint: Follow the motive and the money: who benefits from CAD designs but never asks for a ransom?
objectives: Differentiate threat actor types by motive, capability, and resources
Correlate TTPs with actor profiles

scenarios.title: MFA Bombing at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: A SaaS company's help desk gets a spike of tickets: users report dozens of push-notification MFA prompts at odd hours, and three users tapped 'Approve' just to make them stop. The security team confirms attackers already hold valid usernames and passwords harvested from an earlier phishing wave. The company uses push-based MFA on every login. Leadership asks for the control change that most directly kills this attack.
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest mitigation against this MFA fatigue (push bombing) attack?
evidence: attacker position
The attackers possess valid credentials, so password changes alone do not remove their access path — they can keep triggering pushes.
user behavior
Users approved prompts they did not initiate; training reduced approvals but did not eliminate them.
authenticator options
The identity provider supports number matching on push, and FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys are available to pilot.
choices: Rotate all user passwords and shorten the password expiration policy to 30 days
Deploy phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) and enable number matching on push prompts
Run another round of security awareness training emphasizing 'never approve unexpected prompts'
Block logins from outside the corporate office IP range
scenarios.why: Push bombing works because push approval is phishable and fatigable. FIDO2/WebAuthn is phishing-resistant by design — the credential is cryptographically bound to the legitimate site's origin, so stolen passwords and fake login pages are useless. Number matching forces the user to match a number shown on the login screen, defeating blind 'approve to stop the noise' taps. Training helps but does not fix a weak authenticator; password rotation does not help because the attacker already has working credentials.
scenarios.hint: The weakness is the authenticator itself, not the password. Which authenticator type cannot be phished?
objectives: Evaluate authentication controls against MFA fatigue attacks
Compare phishing-resistant vs phishable MFA factors

domains.name: Threats, Vulnerabilities & Mitigations
domains.summary: Malware families, application and network attacks, password attacks, and vulnerability management — identifying what is hitting you and how to stop it.

scenarios.title: Encrypted by Morning
scenarios.situation: Monday 7:40 AM: the help desk queue fills with the same ticket — 'all my files have a .locked extension and there's a ransom note on my desktop.' Within an hour the file shares show the same pattern, including machines whose users never opened any attachment. The note demands payment in cryptocurrency for a decryption key and threatens to publish the data in 72 hours.
scenarios.prompt: Which malware classification best describes this incident?
evidence: payload
Files are encrypted in place and a ransom note demands cryptocurrency — the classic crypto-ransomware business model, plus a data-leak threat (double extortion).
spread
Infection reached machines with no user interaction — it propagated across the network on its own.
entry
Patient zero was a single workstation; from there it moved laterally without further phishing.
choices: Trojan — it must have been disguised as legitimate software the users installed
Logic bomb — the payload triggered on a timer Monday morning
Crypto-ransomware with worm-like propagation
Rootkit — it hid in the boot sector to survive reboots
scenarios.why: Encrypting files and demanding payment is crypto-ransomware; threatening to publish stolen data adds the double-extortion model. Spreading across the network without user action is worm behavior — a pure virus needs a host file and user action to spread. There is no evidence of a timer (logic bomb), disguised software the user chose to run (trojan), or boot-level stealth (rootkit).
scenarios.hint: Two behaviors, two labels: what encrypts for ransom, and what spreads without user help?
objectives: Classify malware by behavior: ransomware, worm, trojan, rootkit
Recognize double extortion

scenarios.title: The Login That Always Works
scenarios.situation: A penetration test report lands on your desk with a critical finding: entering `' OR '1'='1' --` in the customer portal's username field logs the tester in as the first user in the database. The same report notes the site's search box reflects user input back into the page unescaped, popping a JavaScript alert with `<script>alert(1)</script>`. The developers ask what to fix first and how.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct remediation for these two findings?
evidence: login bypass
The string `' OR '1'='1' --` alters the SQL query logic — a textbook SQL injection in the authentication query.
search box
Unescaped reflection of input into HTML enables reflected cross-site scripting (XSS).
current defenses
The app sits behind a WAF, which the testers bypassed with minor encoding variations.
choices: Tune the WAF with stricter rules — the firewall is the right layer to block injection
Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for all database access and context-appropriate output encoding for reflected content
Require 16-character passwords so injected sessions expire faster
Block the characters ' < > -- in the firewall for all traffic
scenarios.why: Parameterized queries separate SQL code from user data at the database driver level — the definitive fix for SQL injection, immune to WAF bypasses. Output encoding neutralizes reflected XSS by ensuring user input renders as text, not markup. A WAF is defense-in-depth, not a fix: testers already bypassed it. Input blocklists are brittle and break legitimate input.
scenarios.hint: Fix it where the vulnerability lives: how the app talks to the database, and how it renders user input.
objectives: Distinguish SQL injection from XSS
Apply parameterized queries and output encoding as primary fixes

scenarios.title: 2,400 Findings, One Weekend
scenarios.situation: Friday's credentialed vulnerability scan returns 2,400 findings across the estate. Two stand out. Finding A: CVSS 9.8 remote code execution in the internet-facing customer portal, with a public exploit published Wednesday and active scanning observed in firewall logs. Finding B: CVSS 7.5 privilege escalation on an internal print server on an isolated VLAN, no public exploit, vendor patch due next quarter. The change window this weekend fits exactly one emergency patch cycle. The CISO asks which goes first.
scenarios.prompt: Which finding should be remediated first, and what reasoning justifies it?
evidence: finding A
CVSS 9.8 (critical), internet-facing, public exploit available, active scanning seen in logs — exploitability is confirmed, not theoretical.
finding B
CVSS 7.5 (high), isolated internal VLAN, no known exploit, patch already scheduled next quarter.
cvss scope
The CVSS base score measures severity of the vulnerability itself — it does not account for your asset's exposure, business criticality, or active threat intelligence.
choices: Finding B first — a 7.5 on infrastructure you own outright is easier to patch safely
Finding A first — combine the CVSS base score with exposure, exploit availability, and active scanning: risk, not just severity, drives priority
Patch neither — wait for the vendor's quarterly rollup to avoid breaking changes
Finding A first — because 9.8 is numerically higher than 7.5
scenarios.why: Risk-based prioritization layers the CVSS base score with environmental factors: internet exposure, a public exploit, and observed scanning make Finding A the imminent threat. Choosing A 'because 9.8 > 7.5' reaches the right answer for the wrong reason — severity alone ignores exposure and threat intel, and would misfire the next time a critical CVE sits on an isolated, unexploitable asset. Finding B is contained and already scheduled.
scenarios.hint: CVSS base score is severity, not risk. What turns a severe bug into an imminent incident?
objectives: Prioritize vulnerabilities using risk, not CVSS alone
Apply exposure, exploitability, and threat intel to triage

domains.name: Security Architecture
domains.summary: Cloud models and shared responsibility, virtualization, Zero Trust, segmentation, and applied cryptography — PKI, TLS, and key management.

scenarios.title: Whose Patch Is It Anyway?
scenarios.situation: A startup runs its product on two platforms: customer email and docs live in a SaaS suite, and the application itself runs on virtual machines rented from an IaaS cloud provider. After a headline-grabbing hypervisor vulnerability, the CTO asks the security team to confirm who is responsible for patching what.
scenarios.prompt: Under the shared responsibility model, who patches the guest operating systems on the company's IaaS virtual machines?
evidence: saas
For the SaaS suite, the provider manages the application, runtime, and underlying infrastructure — the customer configures access and classifies data.
iaas split
In IaaS, the provider secures the physical hosts, hypervisor, and network fabric; the customer controls everything from the guest OS upward.
hypervisor news
The hypervisor flaw sits below the customer's line of responsibility — but the guest OSes above it are theirs.
choices: The cloud provider — patching is always the provider's job in the cloud
The customer — the guest OS sits above the provider's responsibility boundary in IaaS
Responsibility is split 50/50 on every layer regardless of service model
No one — IaaS guest operating systems auto-patch by default
scenarios.why: The shared responsibility line moves with the service model. In IaaS the provider owns up to the virtualization layer; the customer owns the guest OS, applications, data, and identity configuration. In SaaS the provider owns far more, but the customer still owns its data and access controls. 'The provider patches everything' is the single most expensive misunderstanding in cloud security.
scenarios.hint: Draw the line: in IaaS, the provider stops at the hypervisor. What sits above it?
objectives: Apply the shared responsibility model across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS
Assign patching ownership correctly

scenarios.title: Flat and Ripe for Ransomware
scenarios.situation: An incident review finds ransomware entered through one phishing workstation and reached the backup servers, the ERP system, and the engineering file shares within 40 minutes. The network is a single flat /16: every workstation can reach every server on any port. The perimeter firewall is a modern next-gen unit — it simply never saw the east-west traffic. The architects ask for the structural fix.
scenarios.prompt: Which architectural change most directly limits this kind of lateral movement?
evidence: traffic path
All lateral movement stayed inside the LAN — the perimeter firewall only inspects north-south traffic.
blast radius
One compromised host could reach backup infrastructure, meaning backups shared the same broadcast domain as user workstations.
zero trust principle
Zero Trust assumes breach and verifies every connection — implicit trust based on network location is the vulnerability here.
choices: Buy a larger perimeter firewall with more throughput
Segment the network — isolate servers, backups, and workstations with internal firewalls/ACLs and microsegmentation, enforcing least-privilege east-west rules
Install endpoint antivirus on every workstation
Disable Wi-Fi across all offices
scenarios.why: Lateral movement is an east-west problem; a bigger perimeter firewall still never sees it. Segmentation with internal firewalling and ACLs shrinks the blast radius so one workstation cannot reach backup and ERP systems, and it is the network expression of Zero Trust's 'never trust, always verify.' Endpoint AV is a useful layer but does not fix the architecture; disabling Wi-Fi is irrelevant to wired lateral movement.
scenarios.hint: The firewall never saw the attack traffic. Which direction was the traffic moving?
objectives: Design segmentation to contain lateral movement
Map Zero Trust principles to network architecture

scenarios.title: The Chain Broke at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: After the infrastructure team disabled TLS 1.0 and 1.1 on the internal finance portal, users report certificate warnings and failed logins. You pull the server's certificate chain: the leaf certificate is valid and unexpired, but the intermediate CA certificate expired last week. The team renewed the leaf six months ago and assumed they were done. Packet captures show the TLS handshake failing during certificate validation.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause of the handshake failures?
evidence: chain status
Leaf: valid. Intermediate CA: expired last week. Root CA: valid and in client trust stores.
validation rule
Clients validate the entire chain — every certificate from leaf to root must be within its validity period, or the chain is untrusted.
recent change
Disabling old TLS versions changed the protocol negotiation, but the failures are certificate validation errors, not cipher errors.
choices: The TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecation broke compatibility with older clients
The expired intermediate CA certificate invalidates the entire chain — renew the intermediate and redeploy the full chain
The cipher suite is too weak and must be upgraded to a stronger one
HSTS headers are forcing HTTPS on a misconfigured virtual host
scenarios.why: Chain validation is all-or-nothing: an expired intermediate breaks trust for every leaf beneath it, regardless of the leaf's own validity. Renewing the intermediate CA certificate and serving the complete chain (leaf + intermediates) restores validation. The TLS version change is a red herring — the captures show validation failures, and the expired intermediate predates the change. Going forward, monitor intermediate and root expirations, not just leaf certificates, and prefer short-lived certificates with automation.
scenarios.hint: The client trusts nothing it cannot chain to a valid root. Which link in the chain is broken?
objectives: Diagnose PKI chain validation failures
Distinguish certificate errors from TLS protocol/cipher issues

domains.name: Security Operations
domains.summary: SIEM alert triage, the incident response lifecycle, digital forensics fundamentals, and reading logs like an analyst.

scenarios.title: Ten Failures, Then Success
scenarios.situation: Tuesday 3:12 AM: the SIEM fires a correlation alert — '10 failed VPN logins followed by 1 success for user m.chen, source IP in a country where the company has no offices.' The account belongs to a finance analyst who normally logs in from Chicago between 9 and 5. The night-shift analyst is tempted to close it as 'user forgot password.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first response to this alert?
evidence: pattern
Multiple failures followed by a success is the classic password-spraying / brute-force success pattern, not normal typo behavior.
context
3 AM login from an unusual country for a 9-to-5 Chicago user strongly suggests credential compromise, not travel.
siem role
The SIEM aggregated and correlated the events precisely so analysts investigate — closing without validation defeats the control.
choices: Validate the alert, then contain: disable or force-reset the account, revoke sessions, and escalate per the IR plan
Close the alert — users forget passwords all the time
Reimage the VPN concentrator before investigating
Email the user and wait for a reply before doing anything
scenarios.why: Triage means validate first, then contain. The pattern plus the anomalous context makes credential compromise the leading hypothesis, and the right move is to disable/reset the account and kill active sessions before the attacker pivots. Closing it as user error ignores the SIEM's correlation; reimaging the VPN server destroys evidence and fixes nothing; waiting on email gives the attacker hours of dwell time.
scenarios.hint: The SIEM already did the correlating. What is the analyst's job now — and what does the 3 AM foreign success imply?
objectives: Triage a SIEM brute-force-success alert
Apply validate-then-contain discipline

scenarios.title: Don't Pull the Plug
scenarios.situation: The SOC watches ransomware encrypting a file server in real time. A junior analyst reaches for the power button: 'Kill it before it finishes!' The senior analyst stops them. Memory likely holds the encryption keys and the malware's process artifacts; the file server also hosts the only copy of this week's engineering work, and backups run at midnight — six hours away.
scenarios.prompt: What containment action best stops the spread while preserving forensic evidence?
evidence: volatility
Encryption keys, running processes, and network connections live in volatile memory — powering off destroys them permanently.
spread vector
The ransomware is moving across the network to adjacent shares; cutting network access halts that path.
business need
The un-backed-up engineering work argues against destructive actions; the incident is not yet contained.
choices: Power off the server immediately to stop the encryption
Isolate the host from the network (disable its NIC / apply a quarantine VLAN) while leaving it running, then capture memory
Run a full antivirus scan on the server first to identify the variant
Delete the ransomware executable from the server to stop it
scenarios.why: Network isolation stops lateral movement without destroying volatile evidence — the correct balance of containment and preservation. Powering off kills the encryption keys and process artifacts in RAM (order of volatility: memory before disk). Scanning and deleting files on a live compromised host alters evidence and wastes the containment window.
scenarios.hint: Two goals: stop the spread, keep the evidence. Which action achieves both?
objectives: Choose containment that preserves volatile evidence
Apply order of volatility to live response

scenarios.title: The Forensics That Wasn't
scenarios.situation: After a suspected data theft, a well-meaning IT administrator 'did forensics': they copied files from the suspect workstation over the network to their own laptop, imaged the hard drive the next day, and only then dumped RAM 'for completeness.' No hashes were recorded, no write blocker was used, and nobody documented who handled the drive. Legal now asks whether this evidence will hold up.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with how this evidence was collected?
evidence: order
The admin collected disk before memory — the reverse of the order of volatility (registers/cache, memory, disk, logs).
integrity
No cryptographic hashes (e.g., SHA-256) were taken at acquisition, so nothing proves the copies match the originals.
custody
No chain-of-custody log exists, the drive was handled without a write blocker, and files were copied over a live network — every step altered or un-documented the evidence.
choices: Nothing — the files were recovered and that is what matters
The collection violated the order of volatility, lacked integrity hashing, broke chain of custody, and altered the source — the evidence is unreliable and likely inadmissible
The only mistake was not imaging the drive first — RAM dumps are optional
The mistake was involving IT instead of waiting for law enforcement
scenarios.why: Forensic soundness rests on three pillars, all broken here: collect in order of volatility (most ephemeral first — memory before disk), prove integrity with hashes taken at acquisition and verified at every handling step, and maintain an unbroken chain of custody with write blockers preventing alteration. Copying files over the network from a live system changes timestamps and metadata. Legal hold and documentation are what make technical findings stand up in proceedings.
scenarios.hint: Three pillars: what order, what proof it didn't change, and who touched it.
objectives: Apply the order of volatility
Explain hashing and chain of custody for admissibility

domains.name: Governance, Risk & Compliance
domains.summary: Risk management math and treatment options, security frameworks, control types, and privacy obligations — running security as a program.

scenarios.title: The Server That Can't Be Patched
scenarios.situation: A legacy inventory application has a known critical vulnerability, but the vendor went out of business — no patch will ever ship. The business needs the app for six more months until the replacement goes live; shutting it down now would halt shipping. The risk register entry is open and the CISO asks for a treatment decision.
scenarios.prompt: Which risk treatment best fits this situation?
evidence: avoid
Avoidance means eliminating the risk by shutting the app down — the business has ruled that out for six months.
transfer
Cyber insurance transfers financial loss, not the operational risk of a compromised inventory system.
options
Network segmentation, a WAF in front of the app, and enhanced monitoring are all available this week.
choices: Accept — document the risk and do nothing for six months
Avoid — shut the application down immediately regardless of business impact
Mitigate — apply compensating controls: segment it, WAF it, and monitor it closely until decommission
Transfer — buy a cyber insurance rider and consider the risk handled
scenarios.why: Mitigation reduces likelihood or impact without eliminating the business function: segmentation contains a breach, a WAF blocks exploit attempts, and monitoring shortens dwell time. Acceptance leaves a critical, unpatched exposure untreated; avoidance is off the table per the business; insurance transfers financial consequences but does nothing to stop the compromise.
scenarios.hint: You can't patch it and can't kill it. What reduces the risk while it stays alive?
objectives: Select among accept, avoid, mitigate, and transfer
Design compensating controls for unpatchable systems

scenarios.title: Is the Control Worth It?
scenarios.situation: The risk analyst prices a threat to the server farm: a single incident would cost $50,000 (single loss expectancy), and history suggests one incident every five years (annualized rate of occurrence 0.2). A proposed monitoring control costs $8,000 per year and is expected to cut the frequency to one incident every twenty years (ARO 0.05). Finance asks whether the control pays for itself.
scenarios.prompt: Does the control's benefit justify its cost?
evidence: ale before
ALE = SLE x ARO = $50,000 x 0.2 = $10,000 per year of expected loss.
ale after
With the control: $50,000 x 0.05 = $2,500 per year — a $7,500 annual reduction in expected loss.
control cost
The control costs $8,000 per year, every year.
choices: Yes — any reduction in incident frequency justifies the spend
No — the $7,500 annual risk reduction is less than the $8,000 annual control cost
Cannot be determined without a qualitative risk assessment
Yes — because the SLE of $50,000 exceeds the control cost
scenarios.why: Quantitative risk analysis compares the ALE reduction against the annualized control cost: $10,000 − $2,500 = $7,500 of benefit versus $8,000 of cost. The control loses $500 per year on pure numbers. 'Any reduction is worth it' ignores cost-benefit discipline, and comparing the one-time SLE to the annual cost mixes units. (A qualitative factor — regulatory pressure, say — could still justify it, but the math alone says no.)
scenarios.hint: Compute ALE before and after. Then compare the savings to the price tag.
objectives: Calculate ALE from SLE and ARO
Perform control cost-benefit analysis

scenarios.title: Three Regulators, One App
scenarios.situation: The company is launching a mobile payment app: it stores cardholder data, onboards users in the EU, and markets heavily in California. The compliance team must name the regimes that apply and the headline obligations for each before launch. Engineering proposes 'just follow HIPAA, it's the strictest' — the privacy counsel disagrees.
scenarios.prompt: Which combination of frameworks/regulations actually applies to this app?
evidence: card data
Storing, processing, or transmitting cardholder data brings PCI DSS — tokenization, encryption, and network segmentation for the cardholder data environment.
eu users
EU residents trigger GDPR: lawful basis, data minimization, purpose limitation, breach notification within 72 hours, and rights including erasure.
california
California residents trigger CCPA/CPRA: notice at collection, opt-out of sale/sharing, and data inventory obligations.
hipaa scope
HIPAA covers protected health information held by covered entities and business associates — a payment app handling no health data is out of scope.
choices: HIPAA only — healthcare rules are the strictest, so they cover everything
PCI DSS for the card data, GDPR for EU users, and CCPA/CPRA for California users
SOX — the app processes financial transactions
No regulation applies until the company reaches 10,000 users
scenarios.why: Obligations follow the data and the jurisdiction: cardholder data triggers PCI DSS; EU personal data triggers GDPR; California personal data triggers CCPA/CPRA. HIPAA is scoped to health information, not payments, and 'strictest covers all' is not how law works — each regime has distinct rights, timelines, and enforcement. SOX governs financial reporting controls at public companies, not consumer payment apps.
scenarios.hint: Match each data type and user location to its regulator. Which proposal names a health-data law for a payments app?
objectives: Map data types and jurisdictions to PCI DSS, GDPR, and CCPA
Reject out-of-scope framework substitutions

lessons.title: Security Concepts That Carry the Whole Exam
concepts: The CIA triad is the lens for everything else: confidentiality means only authorized parties can access data (encryption, access controls); integrity means data is accurate and trustworthy (hashing, checksums, digital signatures, change control); availability means systems and data are reachable when needed (redundancy, backups, DDoS mitigation). Exam questions constantly ask which leg a scenario threatens — leaked data is confidentiality, altered data is integrity, an outage is availability.

AAA extends the triad into identity: authentication proves who you are (something you know, have, or are — ideally phishing-resistant), authorization decides what you may do after authenticating (least privilege, role-based access), and accounting logs what you did. Non-repudiation builds on accounting with cryptographic proof — a digital signature — so an actor cannot later deny the action.

Security controls come in flavors you must name precisely. By implementation: technical/logical (firewalls, encryption, MFA), managerial/administrative (policies, risk assessments, training), operational (change management, backup procedures), and physical (locks, badge readers, guards). By purpose: preventive (stop it), detective (find it), corrective (fix it), compensating (alternative when the ideal control is impossible), directive (tell people what to do), and deterrent (discourage attempts).

Threat actors are profiled by motive, capability, and resources. Nation-state/APT groups pursue espionage with custom tooling and extreme patience; organized crime pursues money (ransomware, fraud); hacktivists pursue ideological visibility (defacement, leaks); insiders may be malicious, negligent, or compromised; shadow IT creates unauthorized attack surface; unskilled attackers wield ready-made tools. 'Hacker' is never a sufficient answer — always profile.

Attack vectors are the paths in: phishing (email), smishing (SMS), vishing (voice), spear phishing and whaling (targeted), pretexting (invented scenario), baiting (curiosity lure), tailgating (physical follow-in), watering holes (compromised trusted sites), typosquatting (lookalike domains), and business email compromise (executive/vendor impersonation for fraud). Defense is layered: verification procedures and out-of-band confirmation, phishing-resistant MFA, email authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC), and training measured by simulated-phishing click rates — never training alone.

example.code:
# Inspect where a suspicious link REALLY goes before clicking
curl -sIL "https://example-bank-secure.example/login" -o /dev/null -w "final: %{url_effective}\nredirects: %{num_redirects}\n" --max-time 15
dig +short example-bank-secure.example
example.walkthrough: curl -sIL follows the redirect chain silently and reports the effective final URL and redirect count — typosquatted and lookalike domains reveal themselves here because the final domain will not match the brand's real one. dig +short shows the resolving IPs; brand-new or bulletproof-hosted infrastructure is another red flag. Never fetch the body of a suspected phish in a normal browser — headers and DNS give you the verdict safely.

pitfalls: Confusing integrity with confidentiality — leaked data is a confidentiality failure; altered data is an integrity failure
Treating 'hacker' as one actor type — always profile motive, capability, and resources
Assuming training alone stops social engineering — pair it with technical controls like phishing-resistant MFA
Forgetting that non-repudiation needs cryptography (digital signatures), not just logs
lessons.try_it: Take the last three phishing simulations your org ran (or craft three test emails). For each, name the vector (spear phishing, vishing pretext, smishing), the psychological lever (urgency, authority, curiosity), and the one technical control that would have blunted it even if the user clicked.

lessons.title: Know Your Enemy: Malware, Injection, and Network Attacks
concepts: Classify malware by behavior, not by scary name. A virus needs a host file and user action; a worm self-propagates across networks; a trojan disguises itself as legitimate software; a RAT gives remote control; a rootkit provides stealth and persistence (often at kernel or boot level); ransomware encrypts (crypto) or locks (locker) for payment, with double extortion adding a data-leak threat; keyloggers and spyware steal data; logic bombs wait for a trigger; backdoors provide quiet re-entry.

Application attacks exploit trust in input. SQL injection concatenates user input into queries — the definitive fix is parameterized queries (prepared statements). Cross-site scripting comes in reflected, stored, and DOM flavors — fix with context-appropriate output encoding plus input validation. CSRF rides the victim's authenticated session — fix with anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies. Add directory traversal, buffer overflows (bounds checking, ASLR/DEP/NX), race conditions, replay attacks, privilege escalation, and SSRF. A WAF is defense-in-depth, never the primary fix.

Network attacks target the channel. DoS/DDoS spans volumetric floods, protocol attacks, and application-layer abuse — mitigate with CDNs, scrubbing centers, and rate limiting. On-path attacks (ARP poisoning, DNS poisoning, evil twins, rogue APs) are defeated by mutual authentication and encryption. Add deauthentication attacks, RF jamming, and NFC/Bluetooth attacks (bluesnarfing, bluejacking). Encrypt and authenticate the channel: WPA3, TLS, VPN.

Password attacks exploit human reuse. Brute force tries everything; dictionary tries likely words; credential stuffing replays breached username/password pairs; password spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts to dodge lockouts; rainbow tables precompute hashes (salting defeats them); pass-the-hash reuses the hash itself without cracking. Defenses: MFA (phishing-resistant where it counts), throttling and lockout, breached-password screening, and long unique passwords kept in a manager.

Vulnerability management is a cycle: discover (credentialed scans see configuration and missing patches; non-credentialed scans see what an outsider sees), identify via CVE/NVD, score with CVSS (base = severity, temporal = exploit maturity, environmental = your context), disposition false positives and false negatives, prioritize by risk (exposure + exploitability + asset criticality), then remediate, mitigate, or formally accept. Schedule scans around change windows and always get written authorization first.

example.code:
# Service-version scan of a lab target (get written permission first)
nmap -sV -O -p- --open 192.0.2.10 -oN scan.txt
# Read the essentials from the output
grep -E "^[0-9]+/tcp.*open" scan.txt
example.walkthrough: -sV fingerprints service versions (what is actually listening, not just which ports are open), -O attempts OS detection from TCP/IP stack quirks, -p- --open covers all 65,535 ports but shows only open ones to keep output readable, and -oN saves normal output for your report. The grep pulls the lines that matter for triage: open services with versions to check against CVE/NVD, informing your risk prioritization. Credentialed scans go deeper; this non-credentialed view is what an external attacker sees.

pitfalls: Scanning systems you do not own or lack written permission for — that is unauthorized access
Treating CVSS base score as risk — always add exposure, exploitability, and asset value
Calling everything a 'virus' — worms self-propagate, trojans deceive, ransomware extorts
Relying on a WAF as the fix for injection — fix the code with parameterized queries and encoding
lessons.try_it: Against a lab VM you own, run the nmap service scan above, pick the most exposed service, and look up its CVEs. Write a one-paragraph risk prioritization: CVSS base score, whether an exploit is public, and how exposed the host is.

lessons.title: Building It Secure: Cloud, Zero Trust, and Crypto
concepts: Cloud service models slide the shared-responsibility line. In IaaS the provider secures up to the hypervisor and you own the guest OS upward; in PaaS the provider takes the runtime and you own the app and data; in SaaS the provider owns nearly everything except your data, identities, and configuration. Deployment models (public, private, hybrid, community) change where data lives, not who classifies it. Most cloud breaches are customer misconfiguration, not provider failure — harden identity, storage buckets, and security groups first.

Virtualization concentrates trust in the hypervisor. Type 1 hypervisors run on bare metal; Type 2 run atop a host OS. Threats include VM escape (guest breaks into host), VM sprawl (unmanaged images with stale patches), and snapshot data lingering unencrypted. Containers share the host kernel — lighter than VMs but with weaker isolation — so the host and orchestration plane must be hardened. Secure the virtualization layer first: it is the trust root for everything above it.

Zero Trust (NIST SP 800-207) replaces location-based trust: never trust, always verify. The control plane holds the policy engine and policy administrator (deciding access); the data plane holds policy enforcement points (enforcing it). Principles: assume breach, verify explicitly, least privilege, continuous authentication, and microsegmentation so compromise of one workload does not reach the next. Every connection is authenticated and authorized regardless of where it originates.

Segmentation and resilience make breaches survivable. VLANs, DMZs, and air gaps separate trust zones; jump servers/bastion hosts gate administrative access; firewall types map to layers (stateless packet filters, stateful inspection, NGFW with application awareness, WAF for HTTP, UTM bundles). Resilience: load balancing and clustering for availability, RAID and tested backups (3-2-1, with offline/air-gapped copies that ransomware cannot reach), and hot/warm/cold recovery sites matched to RTO/RPO.

Cryptography essentials: symmetric algorithms (AES-128/256, ChaCha20) use one shared key and are fast for bulk data; asymmetric algorithms (RSA with 2048-bit or larger keys, ECC with 256-bit or larger, Diffie-Hellman) solve key distribution and enable signatures. Hashing (SHA-256/SHA-3) proves integrity — MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security use; always salt password hashes and stretch them with bcrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2, or scrypt. A digital signature is a hash encrypted with the private key. PKI binds keys to identities: CAs issue, RAs vet, CRLs and OCSP (prefer stapling) handle revocation, and TLS 1.3 brings 1-RTT handshakes, forward secrecy, and the removal of weak ciphers.

example.code:
# Inspect a live TLS endpoint: version, cipher, and chain
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3 -servername example.com < /dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 2>/dev/null | grep -E "Protocol|Cipher"
example.walkthrough: The first command completes a TLS handshake and pipes the server certificate into openssl x509, printing subject, issuer, and validity dates — expired intermediates and mismatched names show up immediately. The second extracts the negotiated protocol and cipher: you want TLS 1.2 or higher (ideally 1.3) with a forward-secret AEAD cipher, never TLS 1.0/1.1 or RC4/3DES. -servername sends SNI so virtual-hosted sites return the right certificate.

pitfalls: Encrypting without authenticating — encryption alone does not stop tampering; use AEAD ciphers or HMAC
Deploying a certificate without its intermediate chain — clients must chain leaf to root
Using ECB mode or MD5/SHA-1 for security purposes
Assuming the cloud provider secures your data — you own classification, identity, and configuration
lessons.try_it: Run the openssl inspection against three sites you use. Record TLS version, cipher, and days until leaf expiry. Flag anything below TLS 1.2 — then check whether intermediate certificate expirations are monitored anywhere in your organization.

lessons.title: Running the SOC: SIEM, IR, and Forensics
concepts: A SIEM aggregates logs, correlates events, and alerts on patterns no single source reveals. Feed it firewall and IDS/IPS logs, NetFlow, DNS queries, authentication events, and endpoint telemetry. Core use cases: brute-force-then-success, impossible travel, lateral movement, and data exfiltration spikes. Alert fatigue is the enemy — tune rules, baseline normal, and enrich with threat intelligence. SOAR platforms automate enrichment and playbook-driven response on top of the SIEM.

The incident response lifecycle (NIST SP 800-61) has four phases: Preparation (plans, roles, tools, communication trees, tabletop exercises); Detection & Analysis (triage, validation, scoping — is this an event or an incident?); Containment, Eradication & Recovery (stop the spread, remove the cause, restore service); and Post-Incident Activity (lessons learned, control improvements). Tabletop exercises test the plan before a real incident does.

Containment is a judgment call, not a reflex. Network-isolate the host (quarantine VLAN, disable the switch port, host firewall) to stop lateral movement while preserving volatile evidence; powering off destroys memory-resident keys and process artifacts. Disable compromised accounts, revoke sessions and tokens, block malicious indicators at the perimeter — and weigh business continuity at every step. Document each action with timestamps; your notes become the timeline.

Digital forensics follows the order of volatility (RFC 3227): registers and cache, memory, network state, running processes, disk, remote logs, physical configuration, archival media — most ephemeral first. Image disks through write blockers, hash everything with SHA-256 at acquisition and verify at every transfer, and maintain an unbroken chain of custody: who handled what, when. Issue a legal hold early so nobody deletes evidence. Correlate timelines across endpoint, network, and identity logs — one source rarely tells the story.

Log analysis is the analyst's daily craft. Learn syslog severity levels; Windows Event IDs 4624 (successful logon), 4625 (failed logon), and 4688 (process creation); Linux auth.log for SSH brute force; NetFlow for beaconing and exfiltration volume; DNS logs for tunneling and DGAs. Baseline normal first — you cannot spot abnormal without it. When hunting, pivot: IP to user to host to process, across sources, until the story is complete.

example.code:
# Hunt brute-force logins: top source IPs by failed-password count
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10
# Then check whether any of those IPs later succeeded
grep "Accepted password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort -u
example.walkthrough: The first pipeline filters failed-password lines, extracts the source IP field, and counts occurrences per IP — a sudden spike from one IP is your brute-force or password-spraying indicator. The second lists every IP with a successful login; any IP appearing in both lists is a failures-then-success compromise candidate — exactly the SIEM correlation from the scenarios, done by hand. Cross-reference with GeoIP and your VPN logs before escalating.

pitfalls: Powering off a compromised host before capturing memory — respect the order of volatility
Treating every SIEM alert as an incident — triage: validate, then escalate
Doing forensics without hashing and chain of custody — technically interesting, legally useless
Analyzing one log source in isolation — correlate across endpoint, network, and identity
lessons.try_it: On a Linux lab box, generate 20 failed SSH logins from another host, then run the pipeline above. Tune it: add a threshold (e.g., flag IPs with more than 10 failures) and write offenders to a blocklist file with timestamps.

lessons.title: Running Security as a Program: Risk, Frameworks, Privacy
concepts: Risk management turns fear into math and decisions. Risk is likelihood times impact. Qualitative analysis ranks risks on a matrix (low/medium/high); quantitative analysis computes ALE = SLE x ARO, where SLE is asset value times exposure factor. The risk register tracks each risk with an owner; treatment options are accept (document and sign off), avoid (eliminate the activity), mitigate (reduce likelihood or impact), and transfer (insurance, outsourcing). Whatever remains is residual risk, measured against leadership's risk appetite and tolerance.

NIST CSF 2.0 organizes programs into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Around it: the NIST Risk Management Framework for authorizing systems, SP 800-53's control catalog, SP 800-61 for incident response, and SP 800-207 for Zero Trust. Frameworks organize controls and create a common language — they do not replace judgment about your specific risks.

Industry frameworks overlap heavily — map once, satisfy many. ISO/IEC 27001 defines ISMS requirements (and certification), 27002 gives control guidance; PCI DSS protects cardholder data; SOC 2 reports on service-organization controls; CIS Controls prioritize safeguards into implementation groups IG1–IG3; COBIT governs IT overall. Start from your obligations (contracts, regulators, customers) and map controls to all of them.

Controls need two taxonomies. By implementation: managerial (policies, risk assessments, training), technical (encryption, MFA, firewalls), operational (change management, media handling, personnel security), physical (badge access, cameras, guards). By purpose: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, directive. Policies sit at the top but are not executable alone — they need standards (mandatory rules), procedures (step-by-step), and guidelines (recommended practice) beneath them.

Privacy and data governance decide what you may collect and keep. Classify data (public, internal, confidential, restricted) and attach handling rules to each class. Know PII and PHI; practice data minimization and purpose limitation; define retention schedules and destroy properly (crypto-shredding, degaussing, physical destruction). DLP enforces handling rules technically. Breach notification duties (GDPR's 72 hours, state laws) start the clock at discovery — which is why detection maturity is a privacy control too.

example.walkthrough: This one-liner encodes ALE = SLE x ARO twice — expected annual loss before and after the control — then compares the savings to the control's annualized cost. The verdict rule is the whole discipline of quantitative risk: buy controls whose risk reduction exceeds their cost. Remember the limits: SLE and ARO are estimates, and qualitative factors (regulatory mandates, reputation) can override the math.

pitfalls: Mixing SLE (per-incident) with ALE (annualized) in cost comparisons
Treating risk acceptance as 'do nothing' — it requires documentation and sign-off
Assuming one framework covers all obligations — map each data type and jurisdiction
Writing policies nobody can execute — pair every policy with standards and procedures
lessons.try_it: Pick one real risk in your environment. Estimate SLE and ARO, compute ALE, price one control, and run the verdict. Then write the two-sentence risk-acceptance memo you would file if the math says skip.

labs.title: Network Recon with Nmap
labs.objective: Perform a safe, authorized service-version scan of a lab target and identify exposed services for vulnerability triage.
steps: Confirm you have written permission to scan the target — scanning without authorization is itself an attack. Use your lab VM's address (e.g., 192.0.2.10).
Run a ping sweep to confirm the target is up: nmap -sn 192.0.2.10
Run a service-version scan across all ports, showing only open ones, and save the output: nmap -sV -p- --open 192.0.2.10 -oN scan.txt
Attempt OS detection to inform your triage: nmap -O 192.0.2.10
Extract the open services and versions from your saved output: grep -E "^[0-9]+/tcp.*open" scan.txt
For the most exposed service found, note its exact version — you will check it against CVE/NVD next.

checks.hint: Start with a ping sweep: nmap -sn <target>
Run the service-version scan with -sV and --open
Add OS detection with the -O flag

labs.title: Integrity by Hash: SHA-256 in Practice
labs.objective: Use SHA-256 hashing to prove file integrity and detect tampering — the integrity leg of the CIA triad, hands-on.
steps: Create a test file: echo 'patient dose: 5mg' > dose.txt
Record its baseline hash: sha256sum dose.txt | tee baseline.txt
Verify the file against the baseline: sha256sum -c baseline.txt (expect OK)
Re-verify: sha256sum -c baseline.txt — observe the FAILED result and compare the new digest
Reflect: which CIA leg did the hash protect, and what does this imply for software downloads and forensic images?

checks.hint: Hash the file first: sha256sum dose.txt
Verify against the baseline: sha256sum -c baseline.txt

labs.title: Log Hunting: Brute Force in auth.log
labs.objective: Hunt a brute-force login attack in Linux authentication logs using grep/awk pipelines — the analyst's daily craft.
steps: Simulate an attack from a second lab host (or a partner): generate 25 failed SSH logins against this box.
Count failed passwords per source IP: grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
List every IP with a successful login: grep "Accepted password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort -u
Cross-reference: any IP in both lists is a failures-then-success compromise candidate — escalate it per your IR plan.
Write offending IPs (more than 10 failures) to a blocklist file with timestamps for the firewall team.

checks.hint: Extract the source IP field with awk '{print $(NF-3)}'

sections.heading: Attack types & vectors
items: Phishing (email) / smishing (SMS) / vishing (voice); spear phishing & whaling are targeted
BEC: attacker impersonates an exec or vendor to redirect payments — verify out-of-band
On-path attacks: ARP/DNS poisoning, evil twin, rogue AP — defeat with mutual authentication + encryption
DDoS: volumetric, protocol, and application-layer — mitigate with CDN, scrubbing, rate limiting
Password attacks: brute force, dictionary, credential stuffing, password spraying, rainbow tables (salting defeats), pass-the-hash
Injection: SQLi -> parameterized queries; XSS -> output encoding; CSRF -> anti-CSRF tokens

sections.heading: Malware quick reference
items: Virus: needs a host file and user action to spread
Worm: self-propagating across networks without user help
Trojan: disguised as legitimate software
RAT: remote access and control; rootkit: stealth plus persistence (kernel/boot level)
Ransomware: crypto (encrypts) vs locker (locks); double extortion adds a data-leak threat
Logic bomb: trigger-based payload; keylogger/spyware: silent data theft

sections.heading: Cryptography & key lengths
items: Symmetric: AES-128/256, ChaCha20 — one shared key, fast, for bulk encryption
Asymmetric: RSA with 2048-bit or larger keys, ECC with 256-bit or larger, Diffie-Hellman — key exchange and signatures
Hashing: SHA-256/SHA-3 for integrity; MD5 and SHA-1 are broken — never for security use; always salt password hashes
Key stretching: bcrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2, scrypt
Digital signature = hash encrypted with the private key; verified with the public key
TLS 1.3: 1-RTT handshake, forward secrecy, weak ciphers removed; prefer AEAD ciphers (GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305)

sections.heading: PKI essentials
items: Chain of trust: leaf -> intermediate(s) -> root CA; every certificate must be within its validity period
CRL = downloaded revocation list; OCSP = real-time revocation check; OCSP stapling = server supplies the OCSP response
RA vets identity, CA issues; wildcard covers *.domain; SAN covers multiple names
Protect private keys in an HSM; automate renewal and monitor intermediate expirations too

sections.heading: Incident response phases (NIST SP 800-61)
items: 1. Preparation — plans, roles, tools, communication trees, tabletop exercises
2. Detection & Analysis — triage, validate, scope the incident
3. Containment, Eradication & Recovery — isolate, remove the cause, restore service
4. Post-Incident Activity — lessons learned, improve controls
Contain smart: network-isolate live hosts; never power off before capturing memory

sections.heading: Digital forensics essentials
items: Order of volatility: registers/cache -> memory -> network state -> processes -> disk -> logs
Image disks through write blockers; hash (SHA-256) at acquisition and verify at every transfer
Chain of custody: who handled what, when — unbroken, or the evidence is inadmissible
Legal hold preserves data early; timelines come from correlating logs across sources

sections.heading: Risk management formulas
items: ALE = SLE x ARO (annualized loss expectancy)
SLE = asset value x exposure factor
Buy the control when ALE reduction exceeds annualized control cost
Treatments: accept (document + sign off), avoid (eliminate), mitigate (reduce), transfer (insurance)
BIA: RTO (restore speed), RPO (tolerable data loss), MTD (maximum survivable outage)

sections.heading: Frameworks & regulations
items: NIST CSF 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
NIST SP 800-53 (controls), SP 800-61 (incident response), SP 800-207 (Zero Trust)
ISO 27001 (ISMS certification) / 27002 (control guidance); CIS Controls IG1-IG3
PCI DSS: cardholder data; HIPAA: PHI; GDPR: EU personal data (72-hour breach notice); CCPA/CPRA: California residents
Control types: managerial / technical / operational / physical, each preventive / detective / corrective
